summary: The West Virginia mine wars of 1912-1921, in which coal companies used company stores, debt, private detectives and bought sheriffs against union miners, ending in the armed uprising at Blair Mountain in 1921.

evidence.note: union founding and the 1897 national walkout open the narrative proper
Paint Creek miners issue demands in April 1912, start of the core story
federal troops arrive in September 1921 and the miners' army disbands
Baldwin-Felts mercenaries brought in as strikebreakers
long segment on Matewan police chief Sid Hatfield, the shootout and his assassination
Esau scrip debts repaid through coerced sex with company guards
governor hands county policing to company-aligned state police, martial law follows
armies of thousands, trenches, machine guns and aerial bombing frame it as a civil war
Mingo and Logan counties as the operators' non-union stronghold
armored train machine-guns a miners' tent colony at Holly Grove

notes: civil-war vs protest-revolution is a judgment call: the hosts frame it as a civil war with armies and air power, but it is an armed labor uprising, so both are secondary. Minors among Esau scrip victims are mentioned only briefly, so child-abuse was left out. Sid Hatfield's birth year follows the transcript's age (27 in 1920). The historiography and modern labor coda were treated as too short for reaches_present.
